This starts with lifestyle modifications including a healthy diet, exercise and stopping smoking. A daily baby dose of aspirin along with medications that lower blood pressure and cholesterol may also be used.

related_questions.question: What percentage of carotid artery blockage requires surgery?

text_blocks.snippet: Carotid artery surgery is generally considered when a blockage reaches 70% or more. For symptomatic patients (those experiencing stroke or TIA symptoms), surgery is often recommended for blockages of 50% or greater. The decision to operate depends on several factors, including the severity of the blockage, the presence of symptoms, and the patient's overall health.

list.title: Symptomatic Patients:
list.snippet: If a patient experiences a transient ischemic attack (TIA) or stroke due to a blocked carotid artery, surgery (carotid endarterectomy or stenting) may be recommended for blockages of 50% or greater, with maximum benefit seen in those with 70% to 99% stenosis, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

list.title: Asymptomatic Patients:
list.snippet: For patients without symptoms, surgery is generally considered when the blockage is 70% or more. However, even with less severe blockages, surgery might be considered if the plaque is deemed unstable or if the patient has other risk factors.

list.title: Risk Factors:
list.snippet: The presence of other risk factors for stroke, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking, can also influence the decision to operate.

list.title: Surgical Options:
list.snippet: The two main surgical options are carotid endarterectomy (CEA), which involves surgically removing the blockage, and carotid artery stenting (CAS), which involves placing a stent to open the artery.

list.title: Individualized Approach:
list.snippet: The decision to operate is always individualized, taking into account the patient's specific circumstances and preferences.

text_blocks.snippet: Treatment for a blocked carotid artery, also known as carotid artery stenosis, typically involves a combination of lifestyle changes, medication, and potentially surgical or minimally invasive procedures to restore blood flow and prevent stroke.
snippet_highlighted_words: typically involves a combination of lifestyle changes, medication, and potentially surgical or minimally invasive procedures to restore blood flow and prevent stroke

list.title: Diet:
list.snippet: A healthy diet low in saturated fats, cholesterol, and sodium, and high in fruits, vegetables, and lean protein can help manage cholesterol levels and blood pressure.

list.title: Exercise:
list.snippet: Regular physical activity, such as 40 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise most days of the week, can improve cardiovascular health.

list.title: Smoking Cessation:
list.snippet: Quitting smoking is crucial as it significantly increases the risk of stroke and other cardiovascular problems.

list.title: Weight Management:
list.snippet: Maintaining a healthy weight can also reduce the risk of stroke and other cardiovascular issues.

list.title: Stress Management:
list.snippet: Managing stress through techniques like yoga, meditation, or deep breathing can positively impact cardiovascular health.

list.title: Antiplatelet Medications:
list.snippet: These medications, like aspirin or clopidogrel, help prevent blood clots from forming by reducing platelet stickiness.

list.title: Anticoagulants:
list.snippet: These medications, like warfarin, further reduce the risk of blood clots.

list.title: Statins:
list.snippet: These medications help lower cholesterol levels and can also reduce the thickness of the carotid artery wall.

list.title: Blood Pressure Lowering Medications:
list.snippet: These medications help control high blood pressure, a significant risk factor for stroke.

list.title: Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA):
list.snippet: This is a surgical procedure where the surgeon makes an incision in the neck, opens the carotid artery, and removes the plaque buildup.

list.title: Carotid Angioplasty and Stenting (CAS):
list.snippet: This minimally invasive procedure involves inserting a catheter with a balloon into the blocked artery and inflating the balloon to widen the artery and placing a stent to keep it open.

list.title: Transcarotid Artery Revascularization (TCAR):
list.snippet: This newer procedure involves making a small incision in the neck to access the carotid artery, inserting a stent, and temporarily reversing blood flow to protect the brain during the procedure.

list.title: Regular Ultrasounds:
list.snippet: These are used to monitor the progression of carotid artery stenosis and assess the effectiveness of treatment.

list.title: Close Monitoring:
list.snippet: Patients with a prior stroke, TIA, or significant blockage may require more frequent monitoring and potentially more aggressive treatment.

list.title: Severity of Blockage:
list.snippet: The percentage of blockage in the carotid artery determines the appropriate treatment approach.

list.title: Symptomatic vs. Asymptomatic:
list.snippet: Individuals with symptoms of stroke or TIA, such as weakness, numbness, or vision changes, may require more aggressive treatment.

list.title: Individual Risk Factors:
list.snippet: Factors like age, other medical conditions, and overall health status play a role in determining the best treatment plan.
